lesson.title: Gallbladder and extrahepatic biliary pathways
lesson.summary: The right and left hepatic ducts form the common hepatic duct.

steps.title: Gallbladder and Biliary Tract
steps.body: The gallbladder stores and concentrates bile and lies on the visceral surface of the liver. Right and left hepatic ducts form the common hepatic duct; its junction with the cystic duct forms the common bile duct. The cystic duct permits filling and emptying of the gallbladder.

steps.title: Relationships and functional organization
steps.body: Parts of gallbladder are fundus, body, neck, and cystic duct. Common bile duct is formed by union of common hepatic duct and cystic duct. Common bile duct descends in the hepatoduodenal ligament, passes posterior to the first part of duodenum, then approaches the pancreatic head and second part of duodenum. The fundus projects near the right costal margin at the tip of the 9th or 10th costal cartilage region, depending on surface-anatomy convention.

steps.title: How can one obstruction affect both biliary and pancreatic drainage?
steps.body: The common bile duct and main pancreatic duct usually converge near their entry into the descending duodenum, often through a shared ampullary region. An obstruction near that shared outlet can therefore affect both systems, whereas an isolated cystic-duct obstruction mainly alters gallbladder drainage. The ducts may join in different configurations, so the usual map is not universal. Distinguish the duct carrying bile from the artery supplying the gallbladder: they travel nearby but obstruction has a different meaning in each.

steps.title: Apply the anatomy and resolve a common confusion
steps.body: The right and left hepatic ducts form the common hepatic duct. Joining the cystic duct creates the common bile duct; bile does not have to traverse the gallbladder on its way from liver to duodenum. Flow in the cystic duct can be toward storage or away during emptying. The common bile duct passes behind the proximal duodenum and through or behind the pancreatic head before usually joining the pancreatic duct. Variants are common, so this is the typical pattern.
